claims.source: Consistent with our in vitro studies, transported mRNAs in Drosophila extracts were shown to primarily contain a single mRNA (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012; Soundararajan and Bullock, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in Drosophila extracts.

claims.claim: Two Egl molecules may be required to overcome the auto-inhibition of BicD.
claims.source: Thus, two Egl molecules may be required to overcome the auto-inhibition of BicD, and this is enabled by their simultaneous binding to one mRNA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the stoichiometry data and the bivalent binding model.

claims.claim: The requirement for mRNA is biologically important because it ensures that motor activation is coupled to cargo binding, preventing futile dynein activity.
claims.source: The requirement for mRNA is biologically important because it ensures that motor activation is coupled to cargo binding, preventing futile dynein activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental findings and biological reasoning.

claims.claim: In an actomyosin-based mRNA transport system in budding yeast, mRNA was required for processive motion because mRNA stabilized the interaction of two single-headed class V myosins (Myo4/She3) with the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2 at physiological ionic strength.
claims.source: We previously showed that in an actomyosin-based mRNA transport system in budding yeast, mRNA was also required for processive motion, but for a different reason: mRNA stabilized the interaction of two single-headed class V myosins (Myo4/She3) with the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2 at physiological ionic strength (Sladewski et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sladewski et al., 2013.

claims.claim: In both the dynein-dynactin-BicD and yeast actomyosin systems, the requirement for mRNA ensures that only cargo-bound motor complexes are motile.
claims.source: Although mechanistically the role of mRNA differs from what we show here with dynein-dynactin and BicD, in both cases the requirement for mRNA ensures that only cargo-bound motor complexes are motile.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from comparing the two systems.

claims.claim: The Rab6GTP and CC1 binding sites on CC3 overlap.
claims.source: A competitive mechanism appears to be the case with Rab6GTP, an adaptor protein that links dynein-dynactin-BicD to vesicular cargo. The Rab6GTP and CC1 binding sites on CC3 overlap (Terawaki et al., 2015), implying that both cannot bind simultaneously.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Terawaki et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Rab6GTP (but not Rab6GDP) in solution or bound to artificial liposomes released BicD2 from an auto-inhibited state to promote processive dynein-dynactin motion.
claims.source: Rab6GTP (but not Rab6GDP) in solution or bound to artificial liposomes released BicD2 from an auto-inhibited state to promote processive dynein-dynactin motion (Huynh and Vale, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huynh and Vale, 2017.

claims.claim: Part of the Drosophila BicD CC3 structure has an unusual feature in which the same residues in the two chains of the coiled-coil adopt different heptad registries, referred to as 'heterotypic' interactions.
claims.source: This possibility is due to an unusual feature of part of the Drosophila BicD CC3 structure, in which the same residues in the two chains of the coiled-coil adopt different heptad registries, referred to as 'heterotypic' interactions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of BicD structure from the literature.

claims.claim: The heterotypic region of BicD CC3 may act as a molecular switch to promote weakening of the CC3-CC1 interaction following cargo binding.
claims.source: It was proposed that this region may act as a molecular switch to promote weakening of the CC3-CC1 interaction following cargo binding to the adjacent 'homotypic' segment of coiled-coil (Liu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The function of zip codes in Drosophila appears to differ from that seen in budding yeast, where zip codes in the model mRNA ASH1 are essential for recruitment of myosin motors to the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2.
claims.source: The function of zip codes in Drosophila appears to differ from that seen in budding yeast, where zip codes in the model mRNA ASH1 are essential for recruitment of myosin motors to the mRNA-binding adaptor protein She2 (Sladewski et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sladewski et al., 2013 and comparison with the Drosophila data.

claims.claim: Dynactin can recruit two dyneins to a dynein-dynactin-adaptor protein complex.
claims.source: This result is consistent with recent studies showing that dynactin can recruit two dyneins to a dynein-dynactin-adaptor protein complex (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018), and that complexes with two dyneins show faster movement and enhanced force (Urnavicius et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claims.claim: Complexes with two dyneins show faster movement and enhanced force.
claims.source: This result is consistent with recent studies showing that dynactin can recruit two dyneins to a dynein-dynactin-adaptor protein complex (Grotjahn et al., 2018; Urnavicius et al., 2018), and that complexes with two dyneins show faster movement and enhanced force (Urnavicius et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Urnavicius et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Cryo-EM studies visualized two dimeric dyneins bound to essentially all (>97%) of dynein-dynactin-BicD2N or dynein-dynactin-Hook3 complexes bound to a microtubule in the presence of AMP-PNP.
claims.source: The cryo-EM studies of Grotjahn et al. (2018) visualized two dimeric dyneins bound to essentially all (>97%) of dynein-dynactin-BicD2N or dynein-dynactin-Hook3 complexes bound to a microtubule in the presence of AMP-PNP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grotjahn et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Carter and colleagues found that only 18% of the BicD2N complexes bound two dyneins.
claims.source: Interestingly, Carter and colleagues (Urnavicius et al., 2018) also showed that BicDR1 and Hook3 recruited two dimeric dynein motors, but found that only 18% of the BicD2N complexes bound two dyneins, which they related to the position of the N-terminus of the BicD2N fragment in the complex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Urnavicius et al., 2018.

claims.claim: One factor influencing recruitment of the second dynein to Drosophila BicD is the presence of two bound Egls.
claims.source: Our studies with full-length Drosophila BicD suggest that one factor influencing recruitment of two dimeric dynein motors in an mRNP is the presence of two bound Egls, thus establishing a link between cargo binding and full dynein occupancy on dynactin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data with full-length BicD.

results.result: Full-length BicD exhibits reduced binding to dynein-dynactin compared to truncated BicD constructs. BicDCC1 showed ~10-fold enhanced recruitment to microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin compared with full-length BicD, and mammalian BicD2N showed ~13-fold increase, suggesting evolutionarily conserved auto-inhibition mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by quantitative single-molecule pulldown data shown in Figures 1C and 1D. The similar behavior of truncated Drosophila and mammalian BicD constructs provides strong evidence for conserved auto-inhibition mechanisms. Statistical comparisons and appropriate controls strengthen these findings.

results.result: Full-length BicD adopts an auto-inhibited looped conformation where CC1 interacts with CC2-CC3. Electron microscopy reveals BicD forms a parallel coiled-coil dimer with a characteristic loop structure, with measurements (38.7 ± 3.8 nm from YFP to loop bottom) agreeing with computational predictions (37.7 nm for CC1). Pulldown experiments confirm CC1 interacts with CC2-CC3 but not CC2 alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are well-supported by converging evidence from electron microscopy (Figure 2), quantitative measurements, computational predictions (Paircoil2), and biochemical pulldown experiments (Figure 2F). The agreement between measured and predicted lengths for CC1 strengthens the structural interpretation.

results.result: BicD-Egl complex retains the auto-inhibited loop structure observed in BicD alone. An additional globular structure adjacent to the loop, likely corresponding to the exonuclease homology region of Egl (residues 557-726), is observed in electron microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 3A) showing the loop remains intact in BicD-Egl complexes. The identification of the globular domain as the Egl exonuclease region is reasonable based on known Egl structure, though this assignment is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The auto-inhibited loop of BicD is disrupted only in the presence of both Egl and mRNA. Electron microscopy shows YFP-BicD-Egl-K10min mRNA complexes lack the looped conformation, and single-molecule pulldowns demonstrate K10 mRNA enhances BicD-Egl colocalization with microtubule-bound dynein-dynactin.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by electron microscopy (Figure 3B) and single-molecule pulldown data (Figure 4A,B). The requirement for both Egl and mRNA to disrupt auto-inhibition is demonstrated through systematic comparison of different component combinations.

results.result: Full-length BicD robustly activates dynein-dynactin motility only when both Egl and K10 mRNA are present. Run frequency is minimal without BicD or Egl, low (20% maximal) with BicD-Egl but no mRNA, and enhanced fivefold with K10 mRNA. K10 mRNA lacking the TLS zip code shows reduced activity (35% maximal), similar to heterologous mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 and C56-C60 are supported by run frequency data (Figure 4C) and electron microscopy. The systematic testing of different component combinations provides strong evidence for the requirement of both Egl and mRNA for robust activation. The role of the TLS zip code is demonstrated but not absolute.

results.result: K10 mRNA lacking the TLS zip code causes ~2-fold reduction in BicD-Egl complex association with dynein-dynactin, suggesting Egl binds primarily to the TLS but can also bind weakly to other mRNA regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by single-molecule pulldown data (Figure 4A,B). The partial reduction rather than complete elimination of binding with TLS-deleted mRNA supports the interpretation that Egl has both specific (TLS) and non-specific mRNA binding capabilities.

results.result: The fully reconstituted mRNP (dynein-dynactin-BicD-Egl-K10 mRNA) exhibits motile properties comparable to minimal DDBCC1 and DD(BicD2N) complexes. All three complexes show processive runs of ~5-7 µm at speeds of ~0.4 µm/s, with minor differences in speed and run length between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by quantitative speed and run length measurements (Figure 5B-E) with appropriate statistical tests. The conclusion that the fully reconstituted mRNP is as active as minimal complexes is justified, though some comparisons show marginal statistical significance (p=0.053 for run length in C66).

results.result: Motile mRNPs predominantly contain two Egl molecules (86.7% after correction). Dual-colored Egl complexes move faster and longer than single-colored complexes, suggesting that two Egl molecules favor recruitment of two dimeric dynein motors. When Egl and mRNA are mixed in solution, 83% of complexes contain two Egl molecules.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 are supported by two-color Egl experiments (Figure 6) with appropriate stoichiometry corrections. The bimodal speed distribution and enhanced run lengths of dual-colored complexes provide strong evidence for the functional significance of two Egl molecules. The consistency between motile complexes and solution mixing experiments strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: mRNPs can recruit two dimeric dyneins, with 44% of mRNPs containing two dyneins after correction. Similar percentages are observed for dynein-dynactin-BicD2N (46%) and dynein-dynactin-Hook1 (50%) complexes. Dual-colored dynein complexes move 58% faster and 53% longer than single-colored complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C81 are supported by two-color dynein experiments (Figure 7) with appropriate stoichiometry corrections and statistical analysis. The enhanced speed and run length of dual-dynein complexes is statistically significant (p=0.036 for run length). Comparison with Hook1 and BicD2N provides important context.

results.result: The putative interaction between Egl and dynein LC8 light chain does not affect mRNP motility. mRNPs reconstituted with dynein lacking LC8 show no statistical difference in speed (p=0.57) or run length (p=0.46) compared to wild-type dynein.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by quantitative comparison of WT and LC8-deficient dynein (Figure 8B,C) with appropriate statistical tests. The lack of significant differences in both speed and run length provides strong evidence that the Egl-LC8 interaction is not functionally important for mRNP motility.

results.result: Motile mRNPs predominantly contain one mRNA (89% after correction). Combined with the finding that 87% contain two Egls, this suggests mRNA's function is to ensure recruitment of two Egl molecules to the complex, favoring disruption of BicD auto-inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by two-color mRNA experiments (Figure 9) with stoichiometry corrections. The interpretation that one mRNA scaffolds two Egl molecules is a reasonable inference from the combined stoichiometry data, though the mechanism remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Artificially dimerized Egl (Eglzip) activates dynein-dynactin-BicD in the absence of mRNA, showing motile properties similar to fully reconstituted mRNPs. Eglzip complexes show bimodal speeds (0.43 ± 0.21 and 0.95 ± 0.15 µm/s) and longer run lengths (7.6 ± 0.03 µm) than mRNPs with native Egl-mRNA (5.7 ± 0.09 µm, p=0.03).
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by motility data with the Eglzip construct (Figure 10). This elegant proof-of-principle experiment strongly supports the model that mRNA's primary function is to ensure presence of two Egl molecules. The enhanced run lengths with Eglzip may reflect stabilization of the complex.

results.result: BicD can recruit two dimeric dyneins, resulting in faster speeds and longer runs. Moving complexes predominantly contain two Egl molecules and one K10 mRNA. The mRNA-bound configuration makes Egl bivalent, enhancing its avidity for BicD and ability to disrupt auto-inhibition, as demonstrated by artificially dimerized Egl activating dynein-dynactin-BicD without mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 represent the central mechanistic model and are supported by converging evidence from two-color experiments (Figures 6-9) and the Eglzip construct (Figure 10). The bivalent binding model is a reasonable interpretation of the stoichiometry data, though some aspects remain inferential.

results.result: A single K10 mRNA binds two Egl molecules to create bivalent Egl that disrupts the BicD loop structure, freeing CC1 and favoring recruitment of two dynein motors. This cargo-orchestrated activation ensures only properly cargo-bound motors undergo robust motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 synthesize the major findings into a coherent mechanistic model supported by electron microscopy, stoichiometry data, and the Eglzip experiment. While some aspects are inferential, the model is well-supported by the experimental evidence and provides a satisfying explanation for the observations.

results.result: Background on dynein function and regulation from prior literature. Dynein is the predominant minus-end directed motor but is weakly processive alone. Dynein exists in auto-inhibited states (phi particle, open state) that are relieved by binding to dynactin and adaptors like BicD2N, resulting in highly processive movement with enhanced force production.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C17 summarize established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the current work but represent prior findings rather than new results from this study.

results.result: Background on BicD structure and function from prior literature. BicD2 is composed of three coiled-coil domains with distinct functions (CC1 for dynein-dynactin binding, CC3 for cargo binding). Full-length BicD has mild effects on organelle localization and is assumed to be auto-inhibited, with conflicting prior evidence about which domains interact.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 summarize prior knowledge about BicD with appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for investigating full-length BicD auto-inhibition but represent background rather than new findings.

results.result: Background on K10 mRNA transport system in Drosophila. K10 mRNA is transported by dynein to establish the dorso-ventral axis and contains a TLS element that binds Egl, which binds to CC3 of BicD.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 describe the biological context for the reconstitution system with appropriate citations. This provides important justification for the experimental approach but represents prior knowledge.

results.result: Prior studies show that robust K10 mRNA localization requires the TLS zip code, but even non-localizing mRNAs associate with dynein in Drosophila embryos. Transported mRNAs in Drosophila extracts primarily contain a single mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 and C96 cite prior work that provides important context for interpreting the current findings about zip code function and mRNA stoichiometry. The consistency with prior in vivo/extract studies strengthens the biological relevance of the in vitro reconstitution.

results.result: Discussion of mechanistic implications and comparison to yeast system. Two Egl molecules may be required to overcome BicD auto-inhibition, ensuring motor activation is coupled to cargo binding. This parallels the yeast actomyosin system where mRNA also ensures only cargo-bound motors are motile, though through a different mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 represent reasonable interpretations and comparisons based on the experimental data. The parallel to the yeast system (C99-C100, citing prior work) provides interesting context, though the mechanistic details differ between systems.

results.result: Discussion of alternative cargo-mediated activation mechanisms. Rab6GTP can release BicD2 from auto-inhibition through competitive binding to overlapping CC3 sites. The heterotypic coiled-coil region of BicD CC3 may act as a molecular switch for allosteric regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 discuss alternative mechanisms from the literature with appropriate citations. These provide important context for understanding different modes of BicD activation, though they represent prior work and speculation rather than new findings.

results.result: Discussion of dynein recruitment and comparison to recent structural studies. The function of zip codes differs between Drosophila and yeast. Recent cryo-EM studies show dynactin can recruit two dyneins, with varying percentages depending on the adaptor. The presence of two Egls influences recruitment of two dyneins to full-length BicD.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 discuss the current findings in the context of recent structural studies and other systems. The comparison to cryo-EM studies (C108-C109) that show higher percentages of two-dynein complexes raises interesting questions about experimental conditions and construct differences. Claim C110 represents a key conclusion linking cargo binding to dynein occupancy.
